newsitem.title: USA: U.S., EU deal calls for change in Helms-Burton law.
newsitem.headline: U.S., EU deal calls for change in Helms-Burton law.

text.p: The Clinton administration said on Friday it would seek to change the Helms-Burton law aimed at discouraging foreign investment in Cuba as part of a deal with the European Union to defuse a trade dispute.

The deal calls for the two sides to negotiate a common policy on properties seized by Cuba's Communist government after Fidel Castro took power in 1959. They also agreed to try to globalize "strong standards" on protecting property rights.

The European Union said it will suspend its challenge against the U.S. law at the World Trade Organisation, but reserved the right to continue the case should efforts to negotiate a broad accord protecting property rights fail.

"This understanding will help to promote a transition to democracy and the protection of property rights in Cuba and avoids bringing a foreign policy dispute before the WTO in Geneva," Undersecretary of Commerce Stuart Eizenstat said.
"We will do everything in our power to reach a multilateral agreement on these disciplines, but a final agreement on these issues is not assured," Eizenstat said.

He said two sides will try to reach final agreement by October 15. In the meantime, the White House agreed to seek to change a key provision of the law that bars executives of companies that invest in disputed properties in Cuba from entering the United States. The proposed change would allow President Bill Clinton to waive that provision.

Clinton, who enacted the law last year after Cuba shot down two planes flown by Cuban exiles from Miami, already has authority to waive another provision that would allow U.S. citizens, including Cuban exiles who are now naturalised Americans, to sue foreigners doing business with confiscated property in Cuba. He has twice used that waiver authority.
It is unclear whether the administration will be successful in convincing Congress to change the law.

"I emphasise that Congress is giving up absolutely nothing in exchange for these talks," Sen. Jesse Helms, the North Carolina Republican, said in a statement. "Rest assured that I will monitor these talks closely over the next six months, and will carefully examine any proposed deal that is reached with my House and Senate colleagues at that time."

While Eizenstat and European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan were striving to strike the deal, President Clinton told newspaper editors he would not change the hardline U.S. embargo policy toward Cuba.
"The Castro govenment illegally shot down two planes and murdered Americans," Clinton said.

"Our policy toward Cuba today therefore is one that is dictated by Cuba not by the United States. And until I see some indication of willingness to change it's going to be very difficult to persuade me to change our policy," he said.

In Brussels, European Trade Commissioner Sir Leon Brittan said the deal, struck at noon Washington time after intense talks by telephone, would "chart a path towards a longer-term solution through the amendment of the Helms Burton Act."
Eizenstat said U.S. officials would discuss the agreement with Canada and Mexico, who were also angered by the law.
But Helms had a word of warning for the U.S. neighbours.

"I have a message for our friends in Canada and Mexico: take no comfort from these negotiations," he said. "No matter what their outcome, unless and until you stop trafficking in stolen American property in Cuba, Helms-Burton will continue to apply to you."

The EU was scheduled to file its first brief on its complaint with the WTO on Monday. Eizenstat said that had no deal been reached, discussions would have ended. The United States made it clear it would not cooperate in the case and that it believed the WTO had no authority in what Washington saw as a foreign policy dispute.
Friday's deal bought both sides some time in a dispute that many thought could undermine U.S. support for the WTO.

"What is going on is that both sides are buying time, perhaps hoping to muscle a change in Helms-Burton six months down the road," said Representative Bob Menendez, a New Jersey Democrat who helped broker the enactment of the law last year.

"I doubt that the Europeans will put in the teeth that would ensure compliance by their companies. Unless there are penalties to enforce it, then it won't be worth the paper it is written on," Menendez told Reuters.
